draft.title: Mass defect and binding energy
card: The mass of a nucleus is less than the total mass of its separate protons and neutrons. This difference in mass is called the mass defect.
The missing mass is not lost. It was released as energy when the nucleons joined, and it is found with E = mc².
The binding energy is the energy needed to split a nucleus into its separate nucleons. It equals the energy released when the nucleus forms from them.
A larger binding energy means the nucleus is held together more strongly. In E = mc², m is the mass defect in kg, c is the speed of light and E is in joules.
draft.remember: Mass defect is the missing mass. E = mc² turns it into the binding energy that holds the nucleus together.

a.q: What is the mass defect of a nucleus?
opts: The mass of the separate nucleons minus the nucleus mass
The mass of the nucleus minus the separate nucleons
The mass of the protons only in the nucleus
The mass of the electrons removed from the atom
a.why: A nucleus has less mass than its separate nucleons, so the mass defect is the separate total minus the nucleus mass. The reverse order would give a negative value, and the missing mass is a difference, not the mass of one particle type.
a.clue: Which is smaller: the whole nucleus or its parts added up?

b.q: A nucleus has a mass defect of 3.0 × 10⁻²⁹ kg. Which calculation gives its binding energy in joules?
b.why: E = mc², so the mass defect is multiplied by the speed of light squared. Using c without squaring it gives a value with the wrong size and the wrong units for energy.
b.clue: The speed of light must be squared, then multiplied.

a.best: The mass of the separate nucleons minus the nucleus mass

problems.detail: 'A larger binding energy means the nucleus is held together more strongly' is misleading. How tightly a nucleus is bound is measured by binding energy per nucleon, not total binding energy. A large nucleus such as uranium has a larger total binding energy than iron but is less tightly bound. This also sets up a wrong idea for the fission and fusion point.

'the binding energy that holds the nucleus together' is wrong. The strong nuclear force holds the nucleus together. Binding energy is the energy needed to separate the nucleons, or released when they join, as the card itself says, so the remember line contradicts the card.
The clue 'The speed of light must be squared, then multiplied' gives the answer away. Only one option both squares c and multiplies.

check.summary: Both questions have clear correct answers, but the card wrongly ties total binding energy to how strongly a nucleus is held, rather than binding energy per nucleon. The remember line wrongly says binding energy holds the nucleus together, and the clue for question b gives the answer away.
